extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning discrete mathematics / introductory proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, core properties, and standard proof techniques about functions (relations that are functions), including injective/surjective, composition, inverses, range, restrictions, and common examples/counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of function (total single-valued relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation f from A to B is a function from A to B iff each element of A appears as the first coordinate of exactly one ordered pair in f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes emphasize that the definition requires exactly one image for each a∈A but places no requirement that each b∈B be paired with any element of A; duplicates among second coordinates are allowed and some elements of B may not appear at all. Examples show checking both existence (every a paired) and uniqueness (no a paired with two different b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure modes for being a function
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation fails to be a function if (a) some a∈A is not paired with any element of B, or (b) some a∈A is paired with two different elements of B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example G demonstrates both types of failure: an element of A with no pair and an element of A paired with two different B-elements. When testing a candidate relation, check both coverage of domain and uniqueness of images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function specified by a rule must define values for all domain elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When a function f from A to B is specified by a rule, the rule must determine f(a) for every a∈A (i.e., the rule applies to all a in the domain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes mathematicians sometimes omit the explicit 'for all a∈A' but it is understood; when defining by formula, you must be able to plug in any domain element and get a unique value. Use the rule to generate the set of ordered pairs if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value notation and membership equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: For a function f : A → B and a∈A, b∈B, b = f(a) iff (a,b) ∈ f; f(a) denotes the unique image of a under f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides examples: writing F(1)=5 since (1,5)∈F. This is the standard way to move between set-of-pairs perspective and value-at-a notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two functions equal iff they agree on every input
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem: Suppose f and g are functions from A to B. If ∀a∈A (f(a) = g(a)), then f = g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof method: prove mutual set inclusion by taking an arbitrary element of one function and showing it's in the other via the pointwise equality. Use this theorem as the standard method for proving equality of functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range (image) of a function
rubrics_metrics.description: Ran(f) = { f(a) | a ∈ A }, i.e., the set of all images of elements of A under f; Ran(f) ⊆ B and may be a proper subset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to reason about onto/surjective property; examples show computing range (e.g., set of advisors). Diagrammatic description: second coordinates of ordered pairs in f.

rubrics_metrics.name: Onto (surjective) definition and equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: f is onto iff ∀b∈B ∃a∈A (f(a) = b). Equivalently, f is onto iff Ran(f) = B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove onto, let arbitrary b∈B and construct an a with f(a)=b; to prove not onto, find a specific b∈B not in Ran(f). Example: use algebra to attempt to solve f(a)=x for arbitrary x and identify obstructing x (e.g., division by zero) as witness not in range.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-to-one (injective) definition and equivalent positive form
rubrics_metrics.description: f is one-to-one iff ¬∃a1≠a2 with f(a1) = f(a2). Equivalently: ∀a1, a2 ∈ A ( f(a1)=f(a2) ⇒ a1 = a2 ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof technique: assume f(a1)=f(a2) and derive a1=a2. This positive implication form is recommended for proofs. Examples demonstrate checking injectivity by simple algebra or domain reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of functions yields a function and formula
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : A → B and g : B → C then g ∘ f : A → C, and for any a∈A, (g ∘ f)(a) = g(f(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses existence and uniqueness: for given a choose b=f(a), c=g(b) to get (a,c)∈g∘f; uniqueness uses injectivity arguments on intermediate maps if needed. Also notes composition is associative (from relation composition properties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving relational composition is a function: existence and uniqueness approach
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a relation R from A to C (e.g., g ∘ f) is a function, for arbitrary a∈A prove there exists a c∈C with (a,c)∈R and that such c is unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text repeatedly recommends breaking the proof into existence and uniqueness parts and gives scratch-work planning for such proofs. This pattern applies generally when proving a relation is a function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition preserves injectivity and surjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and g are one-to-one then g ∘ f is one-to-one. If f and g are onto then g ∘ f is onto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof patterns: for injectivity use pointwise implication g(f(a1))=g(f(a2)) ⇒ f(a1)=f(a2) ⇒ a1=a2; for surjectivity, given c∈C use surjectivity of g to pick b and surjectivity of f to pick a with f(a)=b, then (g∘f)(a)=c.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity function properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Identity function i_A : A → A defined by i_A(a) = a for all a∈A is a function that is both one-to-one and onto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use i_A as canonical example of bijection; shown by direct verification. Also used in proofs about compositions and inverses (e.g., f ∘ i_A = f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse of a function is a function iff bijective
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : A → B is one-to-one and onto (i.e., a bijection), then f^{-1} : B → A is a function. Conversely (stated as to be shown later): if f^{-1} is a function then f must be one-to-one and onto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of forward direction separates existence (onto gives a preimage for each b) and uniqueness (injective gives uniqueness). Counterexamples illustrate failures when f is not injective or not surjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction of a function to a subset
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : A → B and C ⊆ A then the restriction f|_C = f ∩ (C × B) is a function from C to B and for all c∈C, (f|_C)(c) = f(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises explore properties: restriction of injective function remains injective; if restriction onto then original may be onto for that codomain; converses may fail—use examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrammatic criteria for injective/onto
rubrics_metrics.description: In arrow/diagram representation: each a∈A has exactly one outgoing edge (function property); injective means distinct a's have distinct targets (no two arrows to same b); onto means every b∈B has at least one incoming arrow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text uses diagrams to illustrate examples and counterexamples; helpful for intuitive checks of injectivity and surjectivity when sets are finite or small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing counterexamples: algebraic strategy for 'not onto'
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a function is not onto, attempt to solve f(a)=x for a general x; identify values of x for which solving fails (e.g., division by zero), and use such a value as explicit witness not in the range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for f(a)=2a/(a+1) solving for a fails when x=2, so 2 ∉ Ran(f). The text recommends trying to prove onto to see obstruction, then turn that obstruction into a counterexample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with equivalence relations and induced maps
rubrics_metrics.description: If R is an equivalence relation on A and f : A → B is compatible with R (i.e., xRy ⇒ f(x)=f(y)), then there is a unique function h : A/R → B such that h([x]_R) = f(x). Conversely, existence of such h implies f is compatible with R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives the standard criterion for descending a function to a quotient set; exercises ask to prove uniqueness and necessity. Use when constructing functions on equivalence classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of functions and condition for being a function
rubrics_metrics.description: Given f : A → C and g : B → C, the union f ∪ g is a function from A ∪ B → C iff f and g agree on A ∩ B (or more generally iff f|(A∩B) = g|(A∩B)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises analyze when f ∪ g is a function and when it is injective in terms of disjointness of ranges. If domains are disjoint, union is automatically a function; if not, need compatibility on intersection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical proof style guidance: prefer positive formulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reexpress negative definitions (e.g., 'no two distinct domain elements map to same value') into equivalent positive implications to ease proving statements (e.g., ∀a1,a2 (f(a1)=f(a2) ⇒ a1=a2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text explicitly recommends using equivalent positive statements for proofs and demonstrates conversion using logical equivalences; used throughout proofs of injectivity and related theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard exercises and verification patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Common verification tasks: determine if given finite relations are functions; compute f(a) for specified inputs; check injectivity/ surjectivity for formula-defined maps; verify properties of compositions, restrictions, unions, induced maps, and equivalence relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises provide examples and counterexamples that illustrate typical pitfalls (domain coverage, uniqueness of image, domain/codomain choices, interplay between injectivity and surjectivity). Use the standard proof templates shown in the chapter.
